name: immutable class
syntax: final class Name { private final T field; }
desc: A class whose state cannot change after construction. Every method that would change it returns a new object instead.
body: The recipe in four steps: the class is `final`, every field is `private final`, there is no setter, and every mutable input is copied on the way in. Methods like `plus` return a new instance, so a shared object can never be edited by one caller behind the back of another. `String` and the record types follow the same idea.

name: defensive copy with List.copyOf
desc: Stores an unmodifiable copy of a collection, so the caller cannot change the object's state through the reference it passed in.
body: Handing out the internal list means any caller can `clear()` it and break the object. `List.copyOf` copies and wraps in one call, and it also rejects `null` elements, which turns a bad argument into an exception at the boundary. For a list that must change later, keep a private `ArrayList` and return `List.copyOf(prices)` from the getter.

name: equals override
desc: Compares content instead of identity. The contract asks for reflexive, symmetric, transitive and consistent behaviour, and no exception on null.
body: `instanceof` with a pattern variable does the cast and the type check in one line, and it returns `false` for `null` without a separate branch. Compare every field that identifies the object, and use the same fields in `hashCode`. Keep those fields `final`: a key whose hash changes after it was put in a `HashSet` is lost inside the set.

name: missing hashCode
desc: Two equal objects must return the same hashCode, otherwise HashMap and HashSet cannot find them again.
body: A hash collection reads the hash first and only then compares with `equals` inside that bucket. Two objects that are equal but hash differently never meet, so `contains` answers `false` while `a.equals(b)` answers `true`. The compiler cannot warn about this, which is why every `equals` needs the matching `hashCode` in the same edit.

name: builder pattern
desc: Collects many optional constructor arguments in a small mutable helper, then creates the immutable target in one validated step.
body: Each setter returns `this`, so the calls chain and the code reads like a sentence. The builder is mutable and short lived; the object it produces is not. Use it when a constructor would need more than about four arguments, or when several are optional and a positional call becomes unreadable.

name: validation in build()
syntax: Target build() { check fields; return new Target(this); }
desc: Keeps every construction rule in one method, so a builder chain cannot produce an object the class would reject.
body: `build()` is the only moment when every field is known, so it is the only place where a rule about two fields at once can be checked. Validating inside each setter also duplicates the code and makes the result depend on which setter ran last. The rule to remember: the builder may hold invalid half state, the built object may not.

name: static nested class
desc: A class declared inside another class with no link to an outer instance. It is used as Outer.Nested and can be created on its own.
body: A static nested class is a normal class that happens to live under another name. It can read the outer class's `private` members when it is given an instance, but it gets no hidden reference of its own. Use it for helpers that belong to the class by meaning: a `Builder`, a `Stats`, a constant table, a small key type.

name: inner class
desc: A non static nested class. Every instance is bound to one outer instance and can read its fields without a getter.
body: Constructing an inner class needs an outer object: `a.review(...)` or the explicit `a.new Review(...)`. The inner object holds a hidden pointer to that `Hotel`, so it can read `name` and `reviews` directly, and it keeps the outer object alive for as long as it exists. If that link is not part of the design, make the nested class `static`.

name: anonymous class
desc: A one-off subclass or interface implementation written where it is used, with no name and no separate file.
body: The class body can use effectively final locals from the method around it. Since Java 8 a lambda replaces the anonymous class whenever the target type has a single abstract method, so `hotels.sort((a, b) -> ...)` is shorter. Keep the anonymous form when the type has several methods, or when you need a real body with fields.

name: record implementing an interface
desc: A record can satisfy an interface through its generated accessors, so records and classes can share one type in a domain model.
body: A record is implicitly `final` and already extends `java.lang.Record`, so it cannot extend a class, but it can implement as many interfaces as you like. `ExtraCharge` gets its two methods for free because the component names are the contract. A record can also override a generated accessor, which is how `amountMinor()` above returns a computed total instead of a stored one.

name: computed total over line items
syntax: long totalMinor() { for (LineItem l : lines) sum += l.amountMinor(); }
desc: One small domain model: an immutable invoice sums polymorphic line items and never exposes its internal list.
body: The arithmetic lives in one method, so a new line type only has to implement `label()` and `amountMinor()` to appear on the invoice. The class owns its list, the records own their values, and nothing outside can edit either. Totals are held in minor units as `long` so the sum never picks up a floating point rounding error.
